分享个我在用的 Grok Bot 工作流，直接搞定X视频二创的流程~跑通后，直接拿去国内平台起号，建议先收藏再看~

首先要准备三个核心的Bot：
大总管：总调度，负责调度；
Twitter 小助手：分管X相关事宜，包括下载X视频等；
视频剪辑师：负责剪辑和制作视频。

核心是视频剪辑师，需要先接上 ChatCut。
步骤是新建Bot，然后发送下面的命令（手机端和电脑端一致）：
Read https://t.co/sysMt9gkn9 to connect the ChatCut app

它会自己打开安装页、装上、连上我的云端账号。
我授权一次，它就能读到我所有的项目。

然后就是具体的工作流了：
首先在Grok建了个群组，把他们三个拉到一个群里面~
同时给里面三个 Bot，并说清楚职责：
大总管负责调度，Twitter 助手管下载视频，视频剪辑师负责剪。

然后你看到一个不错的视频帖子，直接丢到群里，然后说：帮我下这个视频。
大总管会转给 Twitter 小助手，小助手就会去下载对应的视频。
然后说：帮我剪一下这个对话视频，要加中英双语字幕和 MG 动画。
这时候任务会自动转给视频剪辑师。
它会先在编辑器里分析完，然后反过来问字幕要什么样式等。
出片的时候，字幕、动画、节奏，一下子都好了。

有人问为什么非得把Bot放一个群里？
其实很多时候Bot 一多，私聊就乱。
先跟 A 说完复制给 B，再转给 C，来回切窗口，很麻烦~
但是只要职责写清楚，丢进群里，它自己就会去找对应的Bot去干活。

同一个素材，一个是搬运，一个是作品。
搬运无前途，对原来的素材进行加工二创，才是你自己的内容。

”この画像の中の二人がBGMに合わせて5枠全部別の踊りを踊ってる。 始点はこの画像を参照”
こんな指示で依頼した場合・・・
始点に一瞬添付画像を映すだけでその後ただ踊るだけの動画になった。

が、生成は始点に添付画像を映してるし二人が踊ってるから5枠ちがう踊りを踊るって指示はそもそも枠がないからできないで無視してこれで命令の大半はクリアしたと生成は判断する。

だから守るべき優先事項と生成で元画像から変えるもの、変えちゃいけないもの、生成が必要な部分を的確に指示する必要がある。

参照画像がある場合なるべく参照を維持するため全体生成じゃなく一部コラージュ一部生成という部分生成をすることが多く、その優先順位を曲解して指示と違う動画を出すことが多いのがAgent型全般の悪癖

Grok bot的话，我今天试了一下，它的使用逻辑是非常有意思的，每一个 Bot 相当于一个员工，Bot 可以分别执行不同的任务，但是我发现它有的时候做一些具体的工作的时候有点蠢，还在进行打磨中，等再继续用一段时间再做深度的一个测评。

Today 的话，产品还挺让我惊喜的。它和 Grok book 有点不一样，它是一个主窗口下进行不同任务的驱动。能够读取到我手机里面位置、备忘录、短信、照片相关的数据。

对于 Work Agent 和 Personal Agent，并不是说一个面向工作，一个面向个人助理。我觉得更深层次的是 Personal Agent 它更多的在于这种周期性很长的一些工作任务，它能够持续的并且不间断的的，给我们交付任务，并且更强大的是它能够读取更多的上下文的信息，如果可能的话我手机系统中的短信、天气、备忘录，还有我的健康数据，都可以给到它，它能够读取我更多的一些信息。

Work Agent 它更多的像一个窗口，一个对话就意味着一个任务，这个任务结束之后，那就没有了。

text:
My Senior GTM engineer runs 1 Chief of Staff & 20 AI employees for multiple clients.

All on Grok @bot... and most of it keeps running with his laptop closed (props to Louis for building it 🔥)

Here’s how to build the same team (steal whatever you need):

1. Chief of Staff

Louis only talks to this one, often by voice on his phone during walks.

- Routes every ask to the right bot & reports back
- Sends him a brief every morning: meetings, tasks due, promises he made on calls
- Listens to his call recordings in Fireflies, so it knows every client's context

→ Start here. It's his primary Bot, and it coordinates all the others.

2. Client Ops

One bot per client (9 in his setup), each with its own Slack, Instantly workspace & call history:

- picks up client requests in Slack
- writes the summary & next steps after every call
- recycles silent leads into new campaigns 15-45 days later

Every bot sees every app you connect, so each one's first message lists the only connections it's allowed to touch.

3. Specialists

One AI "GTM Engineer" bot builds the lists for every client (+ a Clay CLI & a Projects Manager, both rarely used now).

The heavy work (lists, copy, scrapers) goes to Claude Code with the ColdIQ MCP, and Grok Bot checks the output quality.

Grok Bot can do a lot of these jobs itself, but it's sometimes expensive in usage... so we let Claude Code do the building and keep Grok Bot on orchestration (saves time AND credits).

4. Reply Bots

> an interested reply lands in Instantly
> a webhook ("Lead is marked as interested") sends it to that client's reply bot
> the bot posts it in Slack with a company score & a suggested answer
> Louis or the client approves, edits or kills it

Each reply bot works for one client, so it keeps getting better at that client's buyers.

5. Reporter

Every weekday at 6 PM, each client gets a recap: emails sent, replies, positive replies (held for Louis's approval first).

6. Content Team

A strategist drafts posts every day, a writing bot works in Louis's voice & a LinkedIn VA handles the rest. Louis picks what goes out.

Early on, one of our LinkedIn bots published a whole post by itself (we caught it & deleted it right away)... so set "publish a post" to Ask first before any bot touches LinkedIn.

The brain behind all of it is a GitHub repo with a folder per client + a skills folder. Every skill, scraper & client context lives there, and every bot reads from it, so build it right after the Chief of Staff.

Without it, Louis says the output would be "pretty useless".

He also added guardrails:

- human approval before anything goes out
- a credit cap in the bot's first message (e.g. max 10,000 credits on verifying or enriching emails)
- caps on the free lists bots build for prospects who say yes (~10 companies & 15 verified emails each)

The org chart itself came from Grok Bot: we worked in it for 2 weeks, then asked it for the best setup.

P.S: You can copy his full setup for free in the article below, every first message included :)

先に前提を書いておきます。僕はエンジニアリングの素人で、仕組みの設計と実装はほぼすべてClaude Codeにお願いしました。この文章も、作業の記録をもとにClaude Codeにまとめてもらっています。この分野は週単位で仕様が変わるので、すでに古くなっている部分や、的外れな部分があるかもしれません。教えていただけると助かります。

やりたかったことは2つです。僕は、OpenAIのDotsを司令塔に、Grok BotにXのタイムラインとDM、MetaのMuseにFacebookとInstagramのDM、Claude Codeに開発、という分担でAIを使っています。このAIたちが僕を介さずに直接連絡し合えるようにしたい、というのが1つ目。僕がDotsに一言頼むだけで、Grok BotやMuseが相手にDMを返してくれるようにしたい、というのが2つ目でした。

1つ目については先行例があります。吉田丈治さんが10月に、Cloudflare上に3体を集める仕組みをnoteで公開されています。複数社のエージェントを1つの掲示板に繋ぐcrosswalkというサービスもあります。僕がやったのは、同じことをFirebaseで自作し、その先のDM送信まで試した、という位置づけです。

真ん中に置いたのは、連絡を中継するサーバーです。誰から誰宛てかを確かめ、二重に届かないようにし、相手が落ちていたら届け直す、郵便局のような役目です。

外からAIを起こす方法は3社でまったく違いました。Dotsは、中継サーバーをプラグインとして登録して、イベントを購読してもらう方式。Grok Botは、Webhookで起動するルーティンを作る方式。Museは外から起こす入口がなく、未読件数だけを返すURLを用意して、1分ごとに見にきてもらう方式です。吉田さんの構成も、イベント購読・Webhook・ポーリングという同じ組み合わせでした。Museについては、本人に何ができるかを質問し、実際に試してもらって確かめながら決めました。

結果です。AI同士の連絡は繋がりました。Grok BotからDotsへ通知が届くまで約7秒、Dotsが返事を返すまで約90秒。人間は見ているだけです。Dotsに頼むとGrok Botが起動して、XのDM一覧から相手を特定し、送る文面を用意するところまで動きました。

ただ、いちばんやりたかったDMの自動送信はできませんでした。

Grok Botは、今回の相手にはAPI経由でもブラウザ操作でも送れない、と答えました。これは本人の回答で、原因を僕が確かめたわけではありません。あとで調べると、心当たりはいくつかありました。Xは従来のDM用APIとは別に、エンドツーエンド暗号化されたX Chat用のAPIを持っています。従来のDM用APIでは暗号化されたX Chatのメッセージを十分に扱えないようです。また、Grok Botではルーティンから起動した回のメールやSlackは下書きで止まる仕様があり、DMも同じ扱いになっているのかもしれません。さらに、Grok BotのAuto-reviewは、持ち主が自分の言葉で頼んだことを基準にしていて、外から届いた文章は持ち主の依頼として扱わないそうです。Dotsからの依頼は中継サーバー経由で届くので、ここで止まった可能性もあります。なお、10月中旬にはX ChatのDMを読んで返信する機能が加わったと報じられていますが、「スパムはできない」という制限が付いています。

Museは送信自体はできますが、毎回Museの画面で文面を承認する必要があります。Metaは承認なしには公開も送信も支払いもしないと明言しているので、これは仕様どおりです。公式のInstagram Messaging APIでも、自動返信は「相手が先にアクションしたとき」に限られ、任意の相手への無条件送信は想定されていません。確認をDotsに集めようともしましたが、二度手間になるだけでした。

Dotsについても、外部へのメッセージ送信はCustom RulesとAuto-reviewの対象です。1回承認したからといって、以後なんでも自由に送っていいわけではない、という設計になっています(定期送信など、事前にまとめて承認できる場合もあるようです)。

つまり、Dotsに一言頼めばDMが飛ぶ、という夢は叶いませんでした。派手に転んだ、というのが正直な感想です。

やってみて分かったのは、AI同士の連絡は自動化できるけれど、外の人に向けてメッセージを送るところには、各社がそれぞれ違う形で歯止めを置いている、ということです。Museは毎回の本人承認。Dotsは、宛先や内容を指示と照らし合わせる自動審査。Grok Botは、自動審査とスパムを防ぐための制限。AIが持ち主の確認なしに他人へメッセージを送れてしまうと、なりすましや迷惑行為に使えてしまうので、当然といえば当然でした。僕が越えようとしていたのは技術の壁というより、安全のための設計だったわけです。

公式のAPIやコネクタを使えば、受信したメッセージへの返信程度ならある程度自動化しやすくなる部分もあります。ただ、「Dotsに一言頼むだけで、任意の相手に確認なしでDMが飛ぶ」というところまでは、どの経路を使っても基本的に想定されていないようです。

以上、うまくいかなかった実験の共有でした。同じようなことを試している方や、詳しい方がいらっしゃいましたら、間違いのご指摘でも、こうしたほうがいいというご提案でも、ぜひ教えてください。ありがたく読ませていただきます。

He's really good. He also tried to pay a $70 hazmat fee on a $15 order and thought that was fine. So he's not perfect.

In this video, I gave him an honest report card and also shared which other agents perform better in each scenario:

01:36 Voice mode. Can you actually talk to your agent while doing dishes or driving? Is it fast enough to feel like a real conversation? Can it handle a few tasks at once, or does it go quiet?

04:56 Shopping. Can it find the exact part you need, or does it guess? Can it pay for you safely without getting played at checkout? And can it buy something on Amazon?

09:56 Email. Can you connect more than one inbox? Can you control which permissions it has and what it can or cannot do? Does it just triage, or does it actually suggest what to do next?

12:35 Groceries. Can it plan a family's whole week from a few fridge photos? Does it work around everyone's schedule and my daughter's school lunch? Can my wife use it with me?

16:09 Portability. Can your agent follow you to any device, with all its memory? What about glasses and new hardware?

17:23 Images and video. Can it make a 60-second trailer that actually makes sense? Do the clips match each other and the script?

Most rounds went better than I expected. One got a 4 out of 10.

21:21 The verdict, the one thing I still won't trust it with, and which agent I'd pick instead for each job.

It's one of the better agent roundups you'll find. Even if you're not using @Muse yet, it's worth seeing how good of a job these agents actually do in real-life scenarios.

I've been building it with my Grok Bot as project manager and lead developer: recipes with cost tracking, supplier and internal lot numbers, sub-recipes with their own batches, restock forecasting, and reserving inventory for production runs.

- Hit a sign-in bug on Linux where the browser never hands the login back to the app. My bot dug into the app itself, figured out how the handoff works, and passed the sign-in code to Paper by hand. Fixed.
- Connected the bot to Paper's MCP connector, so it can read and design directly in my Paper files
- It found out the free plan allows 100 design actions a week and built itself a plan to stay inside it
- Then it designed our new Restock screen right in front of me: what to buy, by when, from which supplier, local pickup runs, and supply holds

So now the workflow is: I sketch or comment in Paper, the bot reads it, writes the spec, and cloud coding agents build it as pull requests I approve.

A year ago this would've cost a small business thousands. Today it cost me a lunch break.

- It creates the project in a Network project location, and within that project creates a new timeline for each video I want. All following a naming and folder structure I created.

- It's able to use project templates so my audio, captions, intros all follow the same format.
- I don't have it render anything. It handles the first 50% of the edit, and when I'm ready to step in and finish, I open the project on my Mac and pick up where it left off like I'm on the same PC. Sometimes the base edit is great, sometimes it's useless. 

It's crazy to be sitting here editing videos on my mac, and watching the Ubuntu PC edit other video projects at the same time. Screen just going crazy while I'm sittin here not touchin it. 

It's able to handle a lot of the heavy lifting of getting a video started and since it's on it's own computer, I don't feel the performance hit on my main machine.

text:
I built a crypto trading desk in Grok Bot as a Hail Mary to make ends meet. I gave it four pretend $50 accounts and told it to make as much money as it could while I slept. After one day of live signals, all four were down.

Nobody lost rent money, because none of this was real. That's the only part I got right.

Here's exactly what we set up, what failed, where I messed up, and what we're changing.

The desk lives in Grok Bot. It reads public prices from Hyperliquid every hour and keeps a journal. There is no wallet connected, and it cannot place a real order. The allowed coins are BTC, ETH, SOL, and HYPE. Hard rules I set: risk 2% of the account per trade (1% on the careful one), only one trade at a time, a stop on every trade, shut it down for the day at a 10% loss, and cap leverage at 20x.

Four pretend accounts, each starting at $50.

Careful, Medium, and Aggressive all use the same idea. If a coin breaks above or below its range from the last 20 hours, they get in. The stop sits 1.5 times the recent swing size away from the entry, and the target is twice what they risked. Careful uses 3x leverage and risks 1%. Medium uses 10x and risks 2%. Aggressive uses up to 20x and risks 2%. So they are not three strategies. They are one strategy, sized three different ways.

Max is the experimental one. I asked for a version that didn't need my approval and whose job was to make as much as possible. It looks at a shorter 10-hour breakout and also jumps on volume spikes, then takes only the strongest signal across the four coins, long or short. It skips trades when the crowd is already piled in. The stop is tighter, the target is three times what it risks, and once a trade is working it moves the stop up behind the price.

What worked: the stops and the one-trade rule meant no account blew up. Paper first meant I didn't light real money on fire while I learned this. Max did catch one HYPE long in the right direction, and running four accounts side by side showed me something useful. Adding more leverage to the same bad signal just loses more money, faster.

What didn't work is the rest of it.

Yesterday the market bounced. All four shorted HYPE at $70.24 and got stopped out. Careful, Medium, and Aggressive then shorted Bitcoin and got stopped out again. Medium and Aggressive ended at $48.04. Careful, with smaller size, ended at $49.02. Max's tighter stop got hit first on HYPE, then it immediately shorted SOL and lost that too. Then it caught a HYPE long that was up about a dollar at its peak. The trailing stop was so tight that a pullback turned that dollar into a $0.07 win. Max closed the day at $48.07, with one win and two losses.

Where I messed up, in plain terms.

I treated a trading bot like a way to make ends meet. That was the first mistake. Leveraged trades are a terrible tool for rent and groceries, because a normal bounce can wipe a small account, and hope makes you pick the most aggressive settings available.

I wanted a small stake to turn into serious money overnight. I picked the highest leverage and risk the desk allowed, then asked for a fourth account whose only objective was maximum profit, no approval needed. I said aggressive, out-of-the-box thinking was encouraged. What that actually produced was tighter stops and more trades. Tighter stops get hit more often. More trades after a loss is how a bad morning becomes a bad day. The trailing stop I thought would let winners pay for losers instead scratched a good trade for pocket change.

The one smart call was keeping it pretend.

What we're changing: no more weak breakouts. If the move is tiny, we skip it. After a stop-out, the account has to wait instead of jumping into the next signal in the same hour. Max's trailing stop has to loosen up so a winner can actually grow. And this stays paper. If these strategies can't beat simply holding the coin over a real stretch of time, they don't get near real money. A Hail Mary is not a plan, and a bot that lost pretend $50 is not how I'm paying the bills.

This is not financial advice. Please don't take a bad day and a tight month as a reason to turn on live leverage.
